problem: The formula is written 'bytes sent over T ≤ r × T + b', but r is in bits per second and b is in bits, so the left side must be in bits, not bytes. The worked example right below it correctly works in bits, so the formula line contradicts it and also contradicts the unit-mixing exam trap.
fix: Write it as 'bits sent over T ≤ r × T + b', and keep the term list: r in bit/s, T in s, b in bits, so both sides are in bits.

problem: Step 6 goes from 'spread S = 5 ms, so the playout offset must be D ≥ 5 ms'. That only works here because the smallest delay is 0, so spread and d_max happen to be equal. The correct rule (stated earlier in the text) is D ≥ d_max, the largest delay. Quiz Q3 shows the break: delays are 2, 5 and 4 ms, spread 3 ms, yet a playout offset of 3 ms would play packets 2 and 3 (arrivals 15 and 24 ms) at 13 and 23 ms, i.e. late. A student who follows step 6 sets D = 3 ms and loses packets.
fix: In step 6, use D ≥ d_max = 5 ms. In Q3, say: spread = 5 − 2 = 3 ms, which is the buffering needed beyond the fastest packet; the playout offset from send time must be D ≥ d_max = 5 ms, giving play times 5, 15 and 25 ms. Recommend making the text say plainly: buffer depth = spread = d_max − d_min, playout offset D = d_min + buffer + margin.

problem: The caption and aria say 'two delayed packets', but three packets arrive after their send slot: delays are 0, 2, 5, 0 and 5 ms. Only two of them (P3 and P5) use up the whole 5 ms offset; P2 is 2 ms late.
fix: Say 'three packets arrive late (by 2, 5 and 5 ms); the two 5 ms ones land exactly on their playout slots and none arrives after its slot.'

problem: The list says to record s_i and a_i 'on one clock at the receiver'. A send time is stamped by the sender, so this quietly assumes synchronised clocks; a constant clock offset shifts every d_i equally, which leaves jitter and spread unchanged but makes the absolute mean delay wrong.
fix: Add one line: a fixed clock offset adds a constant to every d_i, so jitter and spread are safe but the mean delay is only meaningful if the clocks are roughly synchronised (for example by NTP or the RTP timestamp mapping).

problem: J = (1/n) Σ |d_i − d̄| is called 'the usual jitter figure'. In the standard RTP practice, jitter is a smoothed mean deviation of the successive transit-time differences, not of delays from the window mean. Students who later read the RTP specification will meet a different formula under the same name.
fix: Keep the mean-deviation definition but label it 'one common teaching measure of jitter' and add that RTP instead smooths the mean of |d_i − d_(i−1)|, so the two numbers are close but not identical.
